metadata.title: ECIS — Episode 7: The Bigger Picture
metadata.color_semantics: Claude fidelity UI beats (B00 ask, B07 verdict, B08 handoff, B09 outro) stay cream/ink/terracotta per CLAUDE-BRAND.md. Body beats (B01-B06) illustrate the mechanism — dark stage (#0a0a0f), same PEDAGOGY-approved deviation as Episodes 1-6. PALETTE NOTE: the ep7 visual briefs claim 'same colors as Ep1-Ep6' but list different hex values; confirmed with the author to keep the ESTABLISHED series palette and honor the briefs' intent over their hex list (mapping table in PEDAGOGY.md). So: keyword blue #3E7CB1, FinBERT teal #3EB8A8, NER amber #D9A757, LLM purple #9B6FD1, triangulator terracotta #D97757, prediction gold #D4A853 (Ep6), extraction blue #3E7CB1, consensus/broad-market neutral grey #7F8C8D. metadata.greeting_note: Plain English hello, narrator is Anjana; no channel handle or brand chip on this build.

beats.narration_text: Six episodes in, ECIS could read a transcript, grade itself, and predict the next quarter. Every one of those judgments looked at one company in isolation. I'm Anjana — this week it starts looking sideways.

show.event: ClaudeComposerAsk: greeting 'Hello, Anjana'; ask types itself
runningText 'widening the frame…'
output lines resolve: 'consensus delta as a prediction feature' / 'surprises get lower confidence' / 'graded against its sector, not the index'

props.command: ECIS scores a company's guidance on its own terms. But a raise means something different if analysts already expected it, or if the whole sector raised, or if a peer moved first. How does the system take that in?
output: consensus delta as a prediction feature
graded against its sector, not the index

beats.narration_text: Hello, Anjana here. Quick recap. ECIS reads earnings call transcripts through four independent readers, triangulates their outputs into a single confidence-scored signal, pre-registers that signal, and grades itself against actual stock movement thirty days later. Last episode, the system added a prediction layer. This week, it learns to see the bigger picture.

show.event: a transcript slides in from the left
four reader nodes light in parallel — keyword, FinBERT, NER, LLM
arrows converge on the triangulator; a signal badge lands: 'raised, 0.82'
the gold prediction node from Episode 6 glows
a 30-day market check resolves with a checkmark
the camera pulls back: five parallel pipelines, one per company, each a miniature of the one above
dotted lines fade in across the pipelines — the hint of correlation

beats.narration_text: A raised guidance signal means more when you know what the market expected. The system now pulls analyst consensus estimates for each company and quarter. It computes the delta: how far the extracted guidance sits from what analysts predicted. That delta becomes a feature in the prediction model.

show.event: left: the extracted guidance badge in extraction blue
right: the analyst consensus estimate in neutral grey
a measuring bar stretches between them; the delta lands in gold
the delta slides down into the feature vector from Episode 6
the vector lights and feeds the gold prediction node

props.sparkLine: How far from what was expected.

beats.narration_text: From that delta, the system computes a surprise score. A company that raises guidance when consensus expected flat produces a high surprise. A raise when everyone already expected a raise scores low. Surprises are harder to predict, so the system assigns them lower confidence.

show.event: left scenario: the company's arrow points up, consensus sits flat — a wide gap
'surprise: high' lands in orange
right scenario: both arrows up, a narrow gap, 'surprise: low' in grey
both scenarios lift; a scatter plot fades in below — surprise on x, confidence on y
dots populate and the cloud slopes downward — more surprise, less confidence
label: 'Harder to predict. Scored accordingly.'

beats.narration_text: Individual signals are useful. Patterns across companies are more useful. The system now computes pairwise correlations between guidance directions across all tracked companies. It identifies clusters that tend to raise or lower guidance together. And it detects which companies signal first. A leading indicator raises guidance one quarter before its peers follow.

show.event: a correlation heatmap builds, Company A through H, filling from top-left
cells shade cool for low correlation, warm orange for high; the diagonal is always maxed
a gold bounding box picks out the co-moving cluster: A, C, E, G
inside the cluster, Company A pulses gold first
a quarter-lag beat, then C, E and G pulse in response
an arrow labels A: 'leads by 1 quarter'

beats.narration_text: The scoring got smarter too. Previously, every signal was graded against the broad market index. But if the entire semiconductor sector rises eight percent and a single company rises five, that is actually underperformance, not confirmation. The system now grades each signal against its sector-specific benchmark. A real test of whether the guidance signal carried information the sector did not already reflect.

show.event: left panel, the old method: company +5% against broad market +2%
green check, 'outperform'
right panel, the new method: the SAME company +5% against its sector at +8%
red cross, 'underperform' — same number, opposite verdict
hold on the contrast
the old panel dims to 30%; the new one brightens
label: 'sector-normalized excess return'

beats.narration_text: Consensus context. Surprise scoring. Cross-company patterns. Sector-aware grading. The system now sees beyond individual signals.

show.event: the full architecture, wide
the consensus delta node glows gold
the surprise badge on the signal output glows
the correlation heatmap thumbnail glows
the sector benchmark node glows, replacing the old broad-market node
all four settle to their resting state
the architecture fades; the title lands: ECIS — Episode 7

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Every judgment the system made before this week looked at one company alone. Now a raise is measured against what analysts already expected, and the further it lands from consensus, the less confident the system is about predicting it. Correlations across companies surface clusters that move together and the peers that move first. And a signal is graded against its own sector, not the index — so beating the market while trailing your sector counts as a miss. Context, not just signal.

show.event: 0.5s lead pause, then ClaudeVerdictArtifact card builds in
line 1: the consensus-delta line settles in
line 2: the surprise/confidence line settles in
line 3: the correlation line settles in
line 4: the sector-benchmark line locks in, largest element

artifactLines: A raise is now measured against what analysts already expected — the consensus delta.
The further a signal lands from consensus, the less confident the system is about predicting it.
Pairwise correlations surface clusters that move together, and the peers that move first.
Signals are graded against their own sector — beating the market while trailing your sector is a miss.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. "I track something where I judge each case on its own — a metric, a team's output, a set of accounts. Can you help me: one, work out what the 'consensus' is in my situation, the baseline everyone already expects, so I can measure how far a result actually lands from it; two, name which of the things I track probably move together, and whether any of them reliably move first; and three, tell me honestly whether I've been grading against the wrong benchmark — beating a broad average while losing to the group I should actually be compared against?" Paste that into Claude and find out whether your own scoreboard has a benchmark problem.

runningText 'checking your benchmark…'
